forces: Soprano, tenor and orchestra; acoustic scoring unestablished
performers: Nellie Melba, soprano; Enrico Caruso, tenor; orchestra uncredited
intro: In the attic, with moonlight falling on Mimì, Rodolfo’s conversation turns into a declaration of love. Nellie Melba and Enrico Caruso sing the duet, at the end of which the new lovers go out into the Paris night.

sections.label: A · Rodolfo and Mimì’s duet
sections.mNote: Rodolfo’s declaration is followed by Mimì’s reply.

sections.label: B · Mimì asks to come along
sections.mNote: The lovers move from declarations to conversation.

cues.title: Duet, opening exchange
cues.text: Rodolfo turns from the window and sees Mimì lit by the moon. He sings “O soave fanciulla, o dolce viso” (“O gentle girl, O sweet face”), and Mimì answers him.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), end of Act I: stage direction and the opening exchange of O soave fanciulla. https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . Translation ours.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Friends in the courtyard
cues.text: Rodolfo’s friends have been shouting from the courtyard, impatient to get to the Café Momus. He tells them to keep two places. As they leave, Marcello calls back that the poet has found his poetry. Upstairs, Mimì stands in the moonlight.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I, the scene immediately before and at the beginning of the duet. https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo

cues.title: Mimì asks to go out
cues.text: Mimì asks to go out with Rodolfo. He suggests that they stay in, because it is cold outside. She promises to stay close to him.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), Act I: Se venissi con voi, Rodolfo’s reply Sarebbe così dolce restar qui and Mimì’s Vi starò vicina. https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: End of Act I, Rodolfo and Mimì
cues.text: Rodolfo helps Mimì with her shawl and offers his arm. Before they leave, he asks her to say she loves him, and she answers “Io t’amo” (“I love you”). They go out together into the cold.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, La bohème (1896), final stage directions and exchange of Act I: https://it.wikisource.org/wiki/La_boh%C3%A8me/Quadro_primo . Translation ours; staging described from the libretto. composer.epithet: Composer who held a theatre audience through a scene of a woman at a window, then brought back a tune it had heard before.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Bazzini and Ponchielli
Giulio Ricordi · Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas, counting Il trittico as three; a Mass, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini began at the organ. His family had supplied Lucca with church musicians for generations, and when his father Michele died in 1864, the five-year-old Giacomo was expected to continue the trade. He studied in the town, played in its churches and completed a Mass in 1880. In 1876, however, he had heard Verdi’s Aida in Pisa, and he turned to the theatre. A scholarship helped him into the Milan Conservatory, where Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli taught him composition. His graduation piece of 1883, Capriccio sinfonico, contains the music that later opened La bohème.

He submitted his first opera, Le Villi, to the Sonzogno competition on the last possible day, 31 December 1883; it did not receive a mention. The librettist Ferdinando Fontana arranged a private hearing at the journalist Marco Sala’s house, with Arrigo Boito among the guests. A subscription paid for a performance at Milan’s Teatro Dal Verme the following May. Giulio Ricordi bought the opera and commissioned another. Edgar, first performed at La Scala in 1889, was a failure that Puccini spent years trying to repair.
